vignette:
Tane is a 63-year-old publisher who came to treatment after years of trying to manage on his own following a man-made disaster at an industry event. He had been attending an evening reception connected to a book fair, the kind of professional gathering where conversation clustered around small tables and drinks were constantly being poured. He remembers the scene in striking visual fragments: the shine of bottles behind the bar, people turning toward a sudden disturbance, the sharp disorganization of the room when panic broke out. What stayed with him was not a blurred impression but a series of crisp, intrusive images that still arrive unbidden, as if the event were stored as pictures rather than a story he can place in the past. Even now, if he tries to speak about what happened, he can feel the memory push forward on its own, clear and detailed in ways he never asked for. Because the pictures came back with so little warning, Tane began trying to manage his days around them, steering away from conversations, rooms, and routines that might give the images a foothold and keeping himself deliberately guarded whenever he could not avoid them.

In the weeks after, Tane found that the memory did not wait for him. He would wake from a nightmare and, before he was fully oriented to his bedroom, the same images would force their way back into his mind. The smell of alcohol was especially potent because it took him straight back to the reception, to the bar area and the sense that danger had erupted in an ordinary social setting. After enough mornings like that, the memory seemed to spread outward into the rest of his life, attaching itself to more and more ordinary cues—the scent of wine at lunch meetings, a colleague's casual question, the hum of a crowded reception—until he felt there were reminders waiting almost everywhere. Being asked about the event by colleagues or family was no better; the act of talking about it seemed to pull the pictures closer and sharpen them. He came to dread these moments because he knew how quickly they could turn into a full reliving of the scene.

What frightened Tane most was how little safety he felt anywhere afterward. He had come to believe that danger could break into even familiar places without warning, and he noticed that he was on guard even inside his own home. Ordinary sounds made him jump—a dropped utensil in the kitchen, a car door outside, the crack of something falling in his office—and the startled surge in his body left him feeling ashamed and exposed. In that state of constant readiness, the memories seemed even more accessible. The more jumpy and watchful he felt, the more easily the event returned in those vivid visual bursts, as though his mind were continually searching for the same threat and finding it in the past.

He responded by organizing his life around vigilance. In restaurants, meetings, and even in his own conference room at the publishing house, Tane always chose a seat with his back to the wall so he could monitor the whole room. Over time, these precautions created their own landscape of reminders: any room where he had to think first about walls, exits, or whether alcohol would be served began to feel marked by the disaster before anything had even happened. He scanned entrances, watched people’s hands, tracked abrupt movements, and avoided seeing friends if he thought the gathering would involve a bar or casual questions about where he had been that night. These habits made sense to him as precautions; he felt he would be foolish not to stay alert. But living this way kept him braced for danger, and the constant checking made the world feel more threatening rather than less. He noticed he was startling more easily and feeling tense at home, as if his own strategies were teaching him that nowhere was truly safe.

The same habits also kept the event mentally alive. By repeatedly surveying rooms and positioning himself defensively, Tane found himself mentally comparing every setting to the reception where the disaster occurred. Entering a crowded launch party for one of his authors, he would immediately look for walls, exits, and signs of trouble, and the old images would rush back with painful clarity. Avoiding friends narrowed his life and reduced the ordinary conversations that might have grounded him in the present; instead, the disaster remained a sealed, highly visual pocket in his mind, ready to intrude. Even his effort not to be caught off guard by waking from nightmares turned into a kind of dread at bedtime, because mornings often began with the memory already pressing in.

At work this has become increasingly costly. As a publisher, he is expected to host authors, attend receptions, and move easily through crowded literary spaces, yet he now arranges himself at the edge of rooms and spends more energy scanning than listening. He has turned down social dinners with colleagues and skipped gatherings with friends, telling himself he is tired or busy. His wife has watched him check locks, react sharply to small noises, and insist on sitting where he can see every entrance, even in their own home. Tane finally sought help after waking from another nightmare and finding that the memory would not loosen its grip for the rest of the day; at a meeting later that morning, the smell of wine from a catered event and a routine question about the disaster left him shaken and mute. He says he is tired of living as if the event is still happening, but he is afraid that if he stops guarding himself, something catastrophic will catch him unaware again.

violations.explanation: The vignette describes intrusive memories and later avoidance/vigilance, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that the memory itself leads Tane to use maladaptive strategies.
The vignette shows triggers bringing back the memory, but does not state that the memory causes or generates triggers/reminders.
The vignette describes maladaptive strategies and mentions trigger-like situations, but it does not explicitly convey in the same paragraph that those strategies lead to or create triggers/reminders.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette describes intrusive memories and later avoidance/vigilance, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that the memory itself leads Tane to use maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette shows triggers bringing back the memory, but does not state that the memory causes or generates triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette describes maladaptive strategies and mentions trigger-like situations, but it does not explicitly convey in the same paragraph that those strategies lead to or create triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
